verses.zh: 成群的民（原文是女子）哪，现在你要聚集成队；因为仇敌围攻我们，要用杖击打以色列审判者的脸。
verses.en: (4:14)[NOTE:1] But now slash yourself,[NOTE:2] daughter surrounded by soldiers![NOTE:3] We are besieged!With a scepter[NOTE:4] they strike Israel’s ruler[NOTE:5] on the side of his face.
notes: Beginning with 5:1, the verse numbers through 5:15 in the English Bible differ by one from the verse numbers in the Hebrew text (BHS), with 5:1 ET = 4:14 HT, 5:2 ET = 5:1 HT, 5:3 ET = 5:2 HT, etc., through 5:15 ET = 5:14 HT. From 6:1 the verse numbers in the English Bible and the Hebrew Bible are again the same.

The Hebrew verb גָדַד (gadad) can be translated “slash yourself” or “gather in troops.” A number of English translations are based on the latter meaning (e.g., NASB, NIV, NLT).sn Slash yourself. Slashing one’s body was a form of mourning. See Deut 14:1; 1 Kgs 18:28; Jer 16:6; 41:5; 47:5.
Heb “daughter of a troop of warriors.”sn The daughter surrounded by soldiers is an image of the city of Jerusalem under siege (note the address “Daughter Jerusalem” in 4:8).
Striking a king with a scepter, a symbol of rulership, would be especially ironic and humiliating. tn Or “staff”; KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT “rod”; CEV “stick”; NCV “club.”
Traditionally, “the judge of Israel” (so KJV, NASB).
verses.commentary:
5:1

NASB
"Now muster yourselves in troops, daughter of troops"

NKJV
"now gather yourself in troops, O daughter of troops"

NRSV
"now you are walled around with a wall"

TEV
"People of Jerusalem, gather your forces"

NJB
"now look to your fortifications, fortress"

Peshitta
"now you shall go forth in a raid"

O daughter of mighty maidens"

This verse is Micah 4:14 in the Hebrew text. There are several translation options:

- The NASB, NKJV, and TEV follow the MT, "gather" (BDB 151 I, cf. Jer. 5:7).

- The Septuagint has "now you are walled about with a wall" (i.e. siege, cf. NRSV, REB). It changes the Hebrew
VERB "gather" (BDB 151, KB 177, Hithpoel IMPERFECT) to a similar Hebrew word
meaning "to build a wall" (BDB 154, i.e. strengthen against a siege, cf. Ezek. 13:5, NJB).

- Another possible translation is "you are slashing yourself, daughter of slashes" (BDB 151, but it would
require a revocalization, cf. JPSOA, Moffatt translation, NET). This last possibility could be accurate because
of the connection between "slashing oneself" and

- idolatry (cf. Lev. 19:28; 21:5; Deut. 14:1; 1 Kgs. 18:28; Jer. 47:5; Hosea 7:14) or

- grief (cf. Deut. 14:1; Jer. 16:6; 41:5; 47:5; 48:37)

The UBS Text Project, p. 319, gives "gash yourself, daughter of a badn" a "B" rating.

Verse 1 describes the situation as it was (Jerusalem about to be sieged), where Micah 5:2-5
describes the situation that will be in the end time (Jerusalem home of the great King). This same temporal
transition can be seen in Micah 5:5-9 in contrast with Micah 5:10-14.

Chapter 4, Micah 5:9-13, deals with Jerusalem. It is possible that 5:1 (MT 4:14) is one
paragraph relating to a besieged capital (Jerusalem). See Contextual Insights, B.

If Micah 5:1 goes with 5:2-5a, then there is a contrast between weak, helpless Jerusalem and
YHWH's new leader from Bethlehem (David's hometown). The Judean monarchy is hopelessly lost in sin and
faithlessness (except for a few godly kings, e.g. Hezekiah, Josiah). YHWH will raise up another faithful king of
David's line, who will fully follow Him (cf. Gen. 49:9-10; 2 Sam. 7; 1 Chr. 17:1)!

▣ "They have laid siege against us" The VERB (BDB 962, KB 1321) is a Qal
PERFECT. Remember the time setting is not in the VERB, but in the context. This
obviously refers to a siege, but which one? There are several theories.

- The historical setting may be Sennacherib's invasion of Judah and his unsuccessful siege of Jerusalem in
701 B.C. ( cf. 2 Kgs. 19:35-36).

- Nebechadnezzar II also invaded and besieged Jerusalem in 586 B.C. (cf. 2 Kgs. 24-25).

- Many scholars believe this may also reflect the future invasion of Jerusalem and destruction of the temple by
Titus in A.D. 70 (cf. Matt. 24; Mark 13; Luke 21); please see my new notes on the Olivet Discourse and
the book of Revelation (2024) online.

Number 1 fits the author's time best, while #3 fits the Messiah's time best.

▣ "With a rod" The term "rod" (BDB 986) meant a stripped tree branch (shorter than a staff) used
as a means of discipline

- for children, Prov. 10:13; 13:24; 22:8,15; 23:13,14; 26:3; 29:15

- as imagery for YHWH's judgment on the nations, Ps. 2:9 (cf. 110:5-6); Isa. 9:4; Rev. 2:27; 19:15

- as imagery for judgment on His own people, Isa. 10:5,24; 14:29

Assyria was called the "rod of God's anger" in Isa. 10:5,24. However, God will also strike Assyria
because of her sins (cf. Isa. 30:31).

"Rod" is also a Hebrew idiom for a king ruling (BDB 986, cf. Micah 7:14; Rev. 2:27; 12:5; 19:15).

▣ "they will smite the judge of Israel on the cheek" "The judge" is a title for the King of Judah, here
called "Israel." To smite one on the cheek was a sign of great insult (cf. 1 Kgs. 22:24; Job 16:10; Lam. 3:30; Acts 23:2),
which shows Babylon's contempt and Judah's weakness.

Rotherham's Emphasized Bible asserts that this judge is the Messiah (p. 887), which
assumes Micah 5:1 goes with chapter 5, not chapter 4.

5:2-5a This whole paragraph marks a radical transition from God's judgment (siege, exile) on Jerusalem and Judah to
God's marvelous restoration (cf. Micah 4:6-8,12-13; 7:18-20). This vacillation is common in prophetic literature and perhaps is

- the work of later editors

- the mind set (antithetical parallelism) of the Hebrew prophets

Special Topic: Eastern Literature (biblical paradoxes)

verses.zh: 伯利恒的以法他啊，你在犹大诸城中为小，将来必有一位从你那里出来，在以色列中为我作掌权的；他的根源从亘古，从太初就有。
verses.en: (5:1) As for you, Bethlehem Ephrathah,[NOTE:1] seemingly insignificant[NOTE:2] among the clans of Judah—from you a king will emerge who will rule over Israel on my behalf,[NOTE:3] one whose origins[NOTE:4] are in the distant past.[NOTE:5]
notes: Ephrathah is either an alternate name for Bethlehem or the name of the district in which Bethlehem was located. See Ruth 4:11.map For location of Bethlehem see Map5-B1; Map7-E2; Map8-E2; Map10-B4.
Heb “being small.” Some omit לִהְיוֹת (liheyot, “being”) because it fits awkwardly and appears again in the next line.
Heb “from you for me one will go out to be a ruler over Israel.”
Heb “his goings out.” The term may refer to the ruler’s origins (cf. NAB, NIV, NRSV, NLT) or to his activities.

In riddle-like fashion this verse alludes to David, as the references to Bethlehem and to his ancient origins/activities indicate. The passage anticipates the second coming of the great king to usher in a new era of national glory for Israel. Other prophets are more direct and name this coming ideal ruler “David” (Jer 30:9; Ezek 34:23-24; 37:24-25; Hos 3:5). Of course, this prophecy of “David’s” second coming is actually fulfilled through his descendant, the Messiah, who will rule in the spirit and power of his famous ancestor and bring to realization the Davidic royal ideal in an even greater way than the historical David (see Isa 11:1, 10; Jer 33:15).tn Heb “from the past, from the days of antiquity.” Elsewhere both phrases refer to the early periods in the history of the world or of the nation of Israel. For מִקֶּדֶם (miqqedem, “from the past”) see Neh 12:46; Pss 74:12; 77:11; Isa 45:21; 46:10. For מִימֵי עוֹלָם (mime ʿolam, “from the days of antiquity”) see Isa 63:9, 11; Amos 9:11; Mic 7:14; Mal 3:4. In Neh 12:46 and Amos 9:11 the Davidic era is in view.
verses.commentary:
5:2 "Bethlehem Ephrathah" Ephrathah (i.e. a clan of the tribe of Judah, cf 1 Sam. 17:12; Ruth 1:2; 4:11;
also note 1 Chr. 2:19,24,50) is added because there was another "house of bread" (Beth-lehem) in the northern tribal allocation
of Zebulun (cf. Josh. 19:15). Bethlehem was known as Ephrath (cf. Gen. 35:19; 48:7; Ruth 4:11). It was a very small village,
only noted because it was the birthplace of King David (cf. 1 Sam. 16:1, and thereby, a way to refer to a future Davidic
Messianic King, cf. 2 Samuel 7; Psalm 89). This verse is quoted in Matt. 2:6 and alluded to in Luke 2:4 and John 7:42.

▣ little" This term (BDB 859 I ) is often used in a pejorative sense of least.

- clans, 1 Sam. 9:21

- tribes, Ps. 68:27

- horns, Dan. 8:9

- towns, Micah 5:2

(list from NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 830)

▣ "clans" The term "clans" is the Hebrew term "thousands" (BDB 48 II). The Hebrew term for
thousand, eleph, can be used as:

- a family or clan unit, Num. 10:4; Josh. 22:14; Jdg. 6:15; 1 Sam. 10:19; 23:23; Micah 5:2; Zech. 9:7

- a military unit, Exod. 18:21,25; Deut. 1:15

- a literal thousand, Gen. 20:16; Exod. 32:28

- a symbol, Gen. 24:60; Exod. 20:6 (Deut. 7:9); 34:7; Jer. 32:18

Bethlehem was so small that she is not even mentioned in Joshua 15 as supplying troops
for the Judean army, or in Nehemiah 11 as supplying workers for rebuilding Jerusalem's walls.

Special Topic: Thousand (eleph)

▣ "of Judah" Because of Moses' prediction about the descendants of Jacob's son, Judah
(BDB 397) in Gen. 49:8-12, esp. v. 10, it became the accepted prophecy that the Messiah would be of
Judah's line, family of Jesse (cf. 2 Samuel 7).

▣ "for Me" This phrase is emphasized in the MT. The Messiah comes at YHWH's bidding. He is
YHWH's full and perfect, human, righteous leader, One who accurately and completely reflects and reveals the God of Israel. The
students of the OT (the rabbis) were not expecting an incarnation (i.e. God becoming a man), but an empowerment
(i.e. like the Judges). God Himself was the true king (cf. 1 Sam. 8:7).

▣

NASB

"His goings forth are from long ago,

From the days of eternity"

NKJV
"Whose goings forth have been from of old.

From everlasting"

NRSV
"Whose origin is from of old

From ancient days"

TEV
"Whose family line goes back to ancient time"

NJB, REB
"Whose origins go back to the distant past,

To the days of old"

JPSOA
"One whose origin is from old,

From ancient times"

Peshitta
"Whose origins go back to the distant past,

Whose goings forth have been predicted from of old,

from eternity"

These two lines are parallel. The VERB, "going forth" (BDB 422, KB 425, Qal
IMPERATIVE) is a very common VERB. It was used in Micah eight times.

- of the Lord coming in Micah 1:3

- of YHWH's law going forth in Micah 4:2

- of repentant Israel being restored in Micah 7:9 (a new exodus, 7:15)

It can refer to the Messiah's origin (NRSV, NJB) or actions (cf. Micah 5:4 and 5a).

These two lines could refer to

- the pre-existence of the Messiah (i.e. as "Wisdom," Prov. 8:22-31 or "the Angel of the Lord"
(see Special Topic: Angel of the Lord);
for pre-existence, cf. John 1:1,14-15; 8:56-59; 16:28; 17:5; 1 Cor. 8:9; Phil. 2:6-7; Col. 1:17; Heb. 1:3; 10:5-7)

- a way of referring to famous descendants of the past (i.e. Abraham, Noah, or more probably, David, cf. Micah 7:14,20; Amos 9:11).

This whole verse alludes to a Davidic king, of David's line, from David's hometown. David was viewed as
the ideal king (cf. 2 Sam. 7; 1 Chr. 17). This means that in this specific context, this phrase could refer back to David's day.

The term "eternity" (BDB 761) is 'olam, which must be interpreted in context. See Special Topic: Forever ('olam and aiōnios).

The NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 347, which discusses 'olam, makes this comment,

"While it is tempting to see here a reference to the eternal preexistence of the
Messiah, no such an idea is found in biblical or postbiblical Jewish literature before the 'Similitudes
of Enoch' (first century B.C. ‒ first century A.D.; see I Enoch 48:2-6."

I think, although there are hints in the OT of an incarnation, the Jewish leaders of Jesus' day were
surprised at His claims of equality with YHWH (e.g. Mark 2:5-7; John 1:1-14; 8:58 and Paul, 2 Cor. 4:4; Col. 1:15; Phil. 2:6;
Titus 2:13). The NT authors see this verse as relating to Jesus' birth (i.e. Matt. 2:6; John 7:42).

A partial list of OT texts that have been used to assert the full Deity of Jesus follows:

- Ps. 2:7, quoted in Heb. 1:5 (see esp. 1:2-3)

- Ps. 45:6-7 quoted in Heb. 1:8-9

- Ps. 110:1 quoted in Heb. 1:13

- Isa. 9:6; Jer. 23:5-6; Micah 5:2 alluded to in Luke 1:32

- Dan. 7:13 quoted in Matt. 26:64; Mark14:62

- Zech. 13:7 quoted in Matt. 26:31; Mark 14:27

- Mal. 3:1 quoted in Mark 1:1-3; Luke 2:26-27

Special Topic: The Trinity

Special Topic: The Bible (its uniqueness and inspiration)

verses.zh: 耶和华必将以色列人交付敌人，直等那生产的妇人生下子来。那时掌权者（原文是他）其余的弟兄必归到以色列人那里。
verses.en: So the Lord[NOTE:1] will hand the people of Israel[NOTE:2] over to their enemies[NOTE:3] until the time when the woman in labor[NOTE:4] gives birth.[NOTE:5] Then the rest of the king’s[NOTE:6] countrymen will returnto be reunited with the people of Israel.[NOTE:7]
notes: Heb “he”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “them”; the referent (the people of Israel) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The words “to their enemies” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
The woman in labor. Personified, suffering Jerusalem is the referent. See 4:9-10.
Gives birth. The point of the figurative language is that Jerusalem finally finds relief from her suffering. See 4:10.
Heb “his”; the referent (the king) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Heb “to the sons of Israel.” The words “be reunited with” are supplied in the translation for clarity.sn The rest of the king’s countrymen are the coming king’s fellow Judahites, while the people of Israel are the northern tribes. The verse pictures the reunification of the nation under the Davidic king. See Isa 11:12-13; Jer 31:2-6, 15-20; Ezek 37; Hos 1:11; 3:5.
verses.commentary:
5:3 "He will give them up until the time" In context the PRONOUN can refer to

- YHWH

- His Messiah

It think it refers to

- YHWH in Micah 5:3, line 1

- but to the Messiah in Micah 5:3, line 3

- is purposeful ambiguity!

The VERB (BDB 678, KB 733, Qal IMPERFECT) is another
very common VERB, which can mean "give," "put," or "set." Here it connotes "deliver up," usually
in a judgment context (cf. Num. 21:3; Jdg. 20:13; 1 Sam. 11:12; 2 Sam. 14:7; 20:21; 1 Kgs. 14:16; Hosea 11:8).

▣ "she who is in labor has borne a child" There are several possible biblical antecedents:

- It goes back to YHWH's first promise of redemption by a male deliverer through a woman in Gen. 3:15; see
Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan.

- It relates to Micah's contemporary, Isaiah, who several years earlier mentioned a special birth (cf. Isa. 7:14; 9:6; 11:1-16).

- It goes back to Micah 4:9-10, which uses the same imagery for Jerusalem's seige and exile, see Special Topic: Birth Pains.

- It relates to the Messianic community (i.e. the faithful remnant; see
Special Topic: The Remnant), as in Revelation 12, bringing forth the Messiah.

The whole point of Micah 5:3 is that God has allowed a limited judgment to overwhelm His faithless covenant people in
order to gloriously restore them (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36; Jer. 31:31-34); Micah 4:1-4; 7:18-20.

▣ "Then the remainder of His brethren

Will return to the sons of Israel" These two lines of poetry may refer to one or two groups:

- "the remnant" (see Special Topic: The Remnant [three senses])

- "the sons of Israel"

- referring to the northern ten tribes (cf. Isa. 10:26-27)

- referring to Judah by the collective title (see Special Topic: Israel [the name])

Historically this would mostly refer to the Judeans taken into exile reuniting with those who
remained in the Promised Land, but eschatologically it refers to "all Israel" (cf. Romans 9-11, esp. 9:6;
John 10:16). The Expositor's Bible Commentary, vol. 7, p. 428, says it refers to "brothers" of the coming
ruler (cf. Micah 5:2). As always, poetic prophecy is brief, ambiguous, and difficult to interpret. It is almost
impossible to interpret without

- a specific historical setting

- a literary context

- OT or NT parallel passages

See D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical
Prophecy and Apocalyptic (this has been a very helpful book for me in interpreting prophecy).

Special Topic: Hebrew Poetry

Special Topic: Prophecy (OT)

▣ "return" There is a play on the word shub (BDB 996, KB 1427, Qal IMPERFECT),
which denotes

- a literal physical returning (from exile)

- a spiritual repentance (from idolatry and rebellion)

This alludes to Micah 2:12-13 and 4:6-8.

Special Topic: Repentance (OT)

verses.zh: 他必起来，倚靠耶和华的大能，并耶和华―他　神之名的威严，牧养他的羊群。他们要安然居住；因为他必日见尊大，直到地极。
verses.en: He will assume his post[NOTE:1] and shepherd the people[NOTE:2] by the Lord’s strength,by the sovereign authority of the Lord his God.[NOTE:3] They will live securely,[NOTE:4] for at that time he will be honored[NOTE:5] even in the distant regions of[NOTE:6] the earth.
notes: Heb “stand up”; NAB “stand firm”; NASB “will arise.”
The words “the people” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “by the majesty of the name of the Lord his God.”
The words “in peace” are supplied in the translation for clarification. Perhaps וְיָשָׁבוּ (veyashavu, “and they will live”) should be emended to וְשָׁבוּ (veshavu, “and they will return”).
Heb “be great.”
Or “to the ends of.”
verses.commentary:
5:4 This is a description of the characteristics of the Messianic reign (cf. Isa. 9:6-7; 11:1-5,6-9,11-16):

- He will stand (i.e. endure or remain, e.g. Ps. 102:26; 111:3,10; 112:3,9; Eccl. 1:4; Isa. 14:26; 66:22; Hag. 2:5)

- He will shepherd His people (David was a shepherd, YHWH is described by him in these terms in Psalm 23, typical ANE imagery for a king)

- He will come in the strength of the Lord

- He will come in the majesty of the name of the Lord, his God

- He will be great

- He will reign to the ends of the earth (BDB 75 e.g. Ps. 2:8; 22:27-28; 59:13; 72:8; see Special Topic: Land, Country, Earth)

- In Micah 5:5, line 1 (which should go with Micah 5:4) He will reign in peace (cf. Micah 5:4, line 4; see Special Topic: Peace (OT))

Notice how Micah 5:4 describes the same time period as Micah 4:1-4.

Special Topic: Messianic Era

5:5a "And this One will be our peace" Peace is the Hebrew word shalom (BDB 1022). It speaks
of wholeness. Jews today use it for a greeting and a farewell. Its eschatological use here is possibly a contrast to
the contemporary false prophets' message of peace (cf. Micah 3:5 and 5:5, line 2, Micah 5:6).

This verse is speaking of a ruler who will bring peace (cf. Micah 5:4) and will himself be called
peace (cf. Isa. 9:6; Eph. 2:14).

Special Topic: Peace (OT, shalom)

verses.zh: 这位必作我们的平安。当亚述人进入我们的地境，践踏宫殿的时候，我们就立起七个牧者，八个首领攻击他。
verses.en: He will give us peace.[NOTE:1] Should the Assyrians try to invade our landand attempt to set foot in our fortresses,[NOTE:2] we will send[NOTE:3] against them seven[NOTE:4] shepherd-rulers,[NOTE:5] make that eight commanders.[NOTE:6]
notes: Heb “and this one will be peace”; ASV “and this man shall be our peace” (cf. Eph 2:14).
Some prefer to read “in our land,” emending the text to בְּאַדְמָתֵנוּ (beʾadmatenu).
Heb “raise up.”
The numbers seven and eight here symbolize completeness and emphasize that Israel will have more than enough military leadership and strength to withstand the Assyrian advance.
Heb “shepherds.”
Heb “and eight leaders of men.”
verses.commentary:
5:5 line 2b-9 Assyria was YHWH's chosen instrument to punish Israel (cf. Isa. 10:5). His covenant
people had gone so far into Ba'al worship they did not know Him (cf. Hosea 11:1-4). He breaks His covenant so
He can reestablish it (i.e. New Covenant of Jer. 31:31-34, described in Ezek. 36:22-36)! Assyria was a limited judgment
(cf. Micah 5:3).

The time frame for this paragraph is uncertain. Assyria may be a way of referring to

- all godly anti-YHWH nations (cf. Zech. 10:10-11), which would be similar to the name Babylon (used in the book of Revelation)

- purposeful ambiguity by specifically mentioning "Babylon" in Micah 4:10 and "Assyria" here.

Special Topic: Kings of Assyria

Special Topic: Kings of Neo-Babylon

5:5 "Then we will raise against him

Seven shepherds and eight leaders of men" Number sequences are common in

- Ugaritic

- OT literature (e.g. Prov. 6:16; 30:15,18,21,29; Amos 1:3,6,9,11,13; 2:1,4,6)

- Ecclesiasticus 11:25

The emphasis is on the adequate number of godly leaders to accomplish YHWH's will who
will be available in that day. Assyria will be judged by Him in the end (cf. Isa. 10:24-27).

There is the question of why does the text have "we will raise" (BDB 877, KB 1086, Hiphil
PERFECT with waw). Does this imply that scattered Israel will be the source of God's
deliverance or is it a way of referring to God's actions (cf.v. 3 line 1) or His Messiah (cf. Micah 5:3 line 3;
Micah 5:4-5 line 1)? This same tension is seen when comparing, "we will raise," Micah 5:5 line 4 and "they will
shepherd," Micah 5:6 line 1 vs. "he will deliver" (BDB 664, KB 717, Hiphil PERFECT with
waw). Micah 5:6 line 3.

The ambiguity of this text and the lack of any historical basis for Jewish soldiers conquering
Assyria cause many (and rightly so) to

- make Assyria stand for any world power who is against God's people

- the conqueror is not "they" but "he" (the ideal ruler of Micah 5:2-5a) will subdue all end-time
opposition (similar to Psalm 2 or Ezekiel 38-39 or Daniel 11:36-45)

verses.zh: 他们必用刀剑毁坏亚述地和宁录地的关口。亚述人进入我们的地境践踏的时候，他必拯救我们。
verses.en: They will rule[NOTE:1] the land of Assyria with the sword,the land of Nimrod[NOTE:2] with a drawn sword.[NOTE:3] Our king[NOTE:4] will rescue us from the Assyriansshould they attempt to invade our landand try to set foot in our territory.
notes: Or perhaps “break”; or “defeat.”
According to Gen 10:8-12, Nimrod, who was famous as a warrior and hunter, founded Assyria.
The MT reads בִּפְתָחֶיהָ (biftakheha) “in her gates,” but the text should be emended to בַּפְּתִיחָה (bappetikhah) “with a drawn sword.”
Heb “he”; the referent (the coming king) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
5:6 "Nimrod" This name (BDB 650) relates to the founding of Babel (i.e. Babylon) and Nineveh
(i.e. Assyria in Gen. 10:8-12). Nimrod is called a mighty hunter who established the first kingdom of
Mesopotamia ("the land between the Rivers," i.e. the Tigris and Euphrates). Therefore, these two terms,
Assyria and Nimrod, are

- simply SYNONYMS

- it refers to neo-Babylon under Nebopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar II

▣

NASB, NKJV
"at its entrances"

NRSV, REB, NET
"with a drawn sword"

NJB
"with naked blade"

JPSOA
"in its gates"

LXX
"with her ditch"

Peshitta
"with their anger"

The MT is reflected by the NASB. JPSOA footnote suggests an emendation to "with drawn
blades" and suggests Ps. 37:14; 55:22 as corroborating texts.

- MT ‒ בפתחיה

- emendation ‒ בפתימה

The UBS Text Project, p. 321, gives the emendation a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

▣ "He will deliver us from the Assyrian when he attacks our land" This is not what happened
in history! Therefore, is this

- a future reference to Cyrus II (i.e. 539 B.C. the city of Babylon falls, cf. Isa. 44-45)

- a reference to the eschatological future (i.e. Messianic period; see Special Topic: Messianic Era)

- a reference to the message of the contemporary false prophets (more probable)

verses.zh: 雅各余剩的人必在多国的民中，如从耶和华那里降下的露水，又如甘霖降在草上；不仗赖人力，也不等候世人之功。
verses.en: Those survivors from[NOTE:1] Jacob will live[NOTE:2] in the midst of many nations.[NOTE:3] They will be like the dew the Lord sends,like the rain on the grass,that does not hope for men to comeor wait around for humans to arrive.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “the remnant of” (also in v. 8).
Heb “will be.”
This could mean “(scattered) among the nations” (cf. CEV, NLT) or “surrounded by many nations” (cf. NRSV).

Heb “that does not hope for man, and does not wait for the sons of men.”sn Men wait eagerly for the dew and the rain, not vice versa. Just as the dew and rain are subject to the Lord, not men, so the remnant of Israel will succeed by the supernatural power of God and not need the support of other nations. There may even be a military metaphor here. Israel will overwhelm their enemies, just as the dew completely covers the grass (see 2 Sam 17:12). This interpretation would be consistent with the image of v. 7.
verses.commentary:
5:7-9 Quite often in Micah (and other prophets) there has been the promise that YHWH would bring
His remnant (see Special Topic: The Remnant (three senses) back to
Jerusalem. However, in this context, He will scatter the remnant of faithful believers throughout the earth that they might

- be a blessing (i.e. "dew from the Lord"), Micah 5:7

- be a champion for justice and godliness, Micah 5:8

If this is accurate then YHWH is using the exiles to scatter His people. His scattered people are His witnesses
to all the nations, which fulfills Gen. 12:2-3; 22:18; 26:4; Acts 3:25; Gal. 3:8!

However, I must admit that it is possible to see both phrases (i.e. Micah 5:7-8) relating to
judgment (cf. Micah 5:9; 2 Sam. 17:12). There is much discussion as to whom this verse refers. Some see it as
scattered Israel, some see it as the end-time people of God (cf. Romans 9-11; 2:28-29; Galatians 3).

It is just possible that this entire context (i.e. 5b-9) reflects the false hopes and predictions
of the false prophets (cf. Micah 3:5). Micah is characterized by radical switching from judgment to redemption. If so,
then Micah 5:1-5a is the true prophet's prediction, while Micah 5:5b-9 relates to false hope of the false prophets!

Special Topic: Why Do OT Covenant Promises Seem So Different from NT Covenant Promises?

Special Topic: YHWH'S Eternal Redemptive Plan

5:7 "dew from the Lord" "Dew" in the OT has several meanings:

- God's blessing, Gen. 27:28; Num. 11:9; Deut. 33:13,28; Prov. 19:12; Hosea 14:5; Zech. 8:12

- lack of it was a divine curse, 2 Sam. 1:21; 1 Kgs. 17:1; Hag. 1:10

- it evaporated quickly in the sunlight, so it was imagery for transient things, Exod. 16:13-14; Isa. 18:4;
Hosea 6:4; 13:3 (similar to mist, vapor, smoke)

- imagery for life or youth, Isa. 26:19

- imagery of pervasiveness, 2 Sam. 17:12

(see Dictionary of Biblical Imagery, pp. 206-207)

verses.zh: 雅各余剩的人必在多国多民中，如林间百兽中的狮子，又如少壮狮子在羊群中。他若经过就必践踏撕裂，无人搭救。
verses.en: Those survivors from Jacob will live among the nations,in the midst of many peoples.They will be like a lion among the animals of the forest,like a young lion among the flocks of sheep,which attacks when it passes through.It rips its prey[NOTE:1] and there is no one to stop it.[NOTE:2]
notes: The words “its prey” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “and there is no deliverer.”
verses.commentary:
5:8 It is obvious that Micah 5:7 and 8 are parallel in structure. The interpretive issue is, are they parallel
in emphasis? Verse 7 seems to be a positive emphasis, but Micah 5:8 seems negative (cf. Micah 5:9).

They may be another example of antithetical parallelism (e.g. Prov. 19:12 uses both "lion"
and "dew"). Dispersed Israel will be both a blessing and a curse. YHWH will bring truth to the nations through
them, but also judgment. Light brings responsibility (cf. Luke 12:48).

▣ "lion" Lion is common imagery for strength and power in the ancient Near East.

Special Topic: Lions in the OT

▣ "there is none to rescue" This is an idiom of divine power (cf. Deut. 32:39; Job 10:7; Ps. 50:22;
Hosea 5:14 and related phrases in Job 9:12; 23:13; and Isa. 42:44).

verses.zh: 愿你的手举起，高过敌人！愿你的仇敌都被剪除！
verses.en: Lift your hand triumphantly against your adversaries;[NOTE:1] may all your enemies be destroyed![NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “let your hand be lifted against your adversaries.”
Heb “be cut off.”
verses.commentary:
5:9 This strophe in verses Micah 5:7-9 is so ambiguous that several theories have been put forth by
translators and commentators. Micah 5:9 may be a clear summary of verses Micah 5:7-8, addressed directly to the
conquering eschatological remnant.

The term "cut off" (BDB 503, KB 500, Niphal IMPERFECT, possibly
in JUSSIVE sense) seems to foreshadow Micah 5:10,11,12,13, which is an obvious judgment
context related to Canaanite societies which trusted in

- its military

- its fortifications

- its religious practices and idols

This false hope and false worship affected many nations in and around Canaan (cf. Gen. 15:16), including Israel and Judah.

verses.zh: 耶和华说：到那日，我必从你中间剪除马匹，毁坏车辆，
verses.en: “In that day,” says the Lord, “I will destroy[NOTE:1] your horses from your midstand smash your chariots.
notes: Heb “cut off” (also in the following verse).
verses.commentary:
5:10-15 YHWH's people were trusting not in Him, but

- in their military might, Micah 5:10

- in their fortifications, Micah 5:11

- their sorceries, Micah 5:12

- their idolatry, Micah 5:13-14 (e.g. Isa. 2:8)

YHWH must stop this by asserting His power and will. This repeated use of "I" reminds me of
Ezek. 36:22-36 (description of the New Covenant of Jer. 31:31-34).

5:10 "in that day" This is a reference to God's judgment day (see note at Micah 4:1, 6).

Special Topic: That Day

The VERB (BDB 503, KB 500, Hiphil PERFECT with waw)
in the Hiphil form is common imagery ("cut off") for a complete destruction and removal (e.g. Micah 5:9,10,11,12,13;
Isa. 9:14; 10:7; 14:22; Amos 1:5,8; 2:3; Zech. 9:10).

▣ "your horses" YHWH's people (i.e. kings), against the direct commands from Him (cf. Deut. 17:16),
went to Egypt to multiply their military power (i.e. chariots). This need not be literal, but stands for a reliance on military power
instead of God (cf. Zech. 9:10), in every age!

▣ "chariots" Chariots were the ultimate weapon of that day. They seem to have been introduced
into this area (originally from the Hyksos rulers in Egypt) by the Phoenicians or Philistines who plated them with iron and
made them the most formidable weapon available (at least on flat ground).

Special Topic: Chariots

verses.en: I will destroy the cities of your landand tear down all your fortresses.
verses.commentary:
5:11 "And tear down all your fortifications" We know from Assyrian documents that in 701 B.C.
Sennacherib captured forty six walled cities of Judah (cf. Micah 5:14b).

verses.zh: 又必除掉你手中的邪术；你那里也不再有占卜的。
verses.en: I will remove the sorcery[NOTE:1] that you practice,[NOTE:2] and you will no longer have omen readers living among you.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “magic charms” (so NCV, TEV); NIV, NLT “witchcraft”; NAB “the means of divination.” The precise meaning of this Hebrew word is uncertain, but note its use in Isa 47:9, 12.
Heb “from your hands.”
Heb “and you will not have omen-readers.”
verses.commentary:
5:12 "sorceries. . .fortune tellers" Micah 5:12-14 refers to the activity of sorcerers (BDB 506, KB 503, attempting
to know and control the future) among the people of God. They are condemned in Lev. 19:26 and Deut. 18:9-22. See
full note in Deuteronomy 18. Many were brought into Israel by Jezebel (cf. 2 Kgs. 9:22).

Special Topic: Magic

▣ "from your hand" This may refer to bracelets, amulets worn by followers. NET Bible has "magic charms." But,
the LXX and Peshitta see the phrase as imagery for "among you" or "in your midst."

verses.zh: 我必从你中间除灭雕刻的偶像和柱像，你就不再跪拜自己手所造的。
verses.en: I will remove your idols and sacred pillars from your midst;you will no longer worship what your own hands made.
verses.commentary:
5:13 "carved images. . .sacred pillars. . .the work of your hands" These refer to various idols which
the people of God were worshiping (cf. Gen. 28:18,22; Deut. 16:22).

Special Topic: Idolatry

verses.zh: 我必从你中间拔出木偶，又毁灭你的城邑。
verses.en: I will uproot your images of Asherah[NOTE:1] from your midstand destroy your idols.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “Asherah poles.”sn Asherah was a leading deity of the Canaanite pantheon, wife/sister of El and goddess of fertility. She was commonly worshiped at shrines in or near groves of evergreen trees, or, failing that, at places marked by wooden poles. These were to be burned or cut down (Deut 12:3; 16:21; Judg 6:25, 28, 30; 2 Kgs 18:4). The Lord states that he will destroy these images, something the Israelites themselves should have done but failed to do.
The MT reads “your cities,” but many emend the text to צִרֶיךָ (tsirekha, “your images”) or עֲצַבֶּיךָ (ʿatsbbekha, “your idols”).

This refers to some type of wooden pole (BDB 81, i.e. carved stake or live tree
representing the tree of life) positioned next to the uplifted rock on Ba'al platforms (i.e. heights). It
represented the female fertility god of Canaan (e.g. Deut. 7:5; 12:3; 16:21; Jdg. 3:7; 6:25,26; 1 Kgs. 14:23;
2 Kgs. 17:10; 18:4; 2 Chr. 31:1), while the sacred pillars of Micah 5:13 refer to the male fertility god
(i.e. Ba'al). These foreign fertility gods and goddesses were introduced from Phoenicia (Jezebel)
and were very popular among the people of God (cf 1 Kings 18-19).

verses.zh: 我也必在怒气和忿怒中向那不听从的列国施报。
verses.en: With furious anger I will carry out vengeanceon the nations that do not obey me.”
verses.commentary:
5:15 "I will execute vengeance in anger and wrath" The terms (plus PREPOSITION "in")
"anger" (BDB 60 I) and "wrath" (BDB 404) are hendiays which intensify the meaning (i.e. in great wrath).

Another option is to see Micah 5:15 as a separate thought. YHWH will purify and restore His
covenant exiled people, but for those of the nations that do not respond (cf. Micah 5:7) He will destroy all idolaters.

▣ "On the nations which have not obeyed" The VERB (BDB 1033, KB 1570,
Qal PERFECT) means to hear so as to obey. See note at Micah 4:1. The same term, but in an
IMPERATIVE form, is repeated in Micah 6:1.

The nations who heard of YHWH from the scattered, exiled covenant people must respond
to the truth they have heard (cf. Micah 5:7).

This seems to be completely out of context with the previous passage, however, it
does emphasize the truth that YHWH does not play favorites with nations, even Israel and Judah. He is
God of all the earth, but only the covenant people had His true word through His true prophets.

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own
interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- Why is it so important that Micah, who lived 750 years before the birth of Jesus, was able to pinpoint the exact location of His birth?

- Why are Micah 5:7-9 so unusual in the context of 8th century prophets?

- How is our country so like Israel in connection with Micah 5:10-14?

- How do you explain the similarity of Isaiah 2:6-8 with Micah 5:10-14?

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us
must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing
is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- Micah contains many very specific prophecies. See Introduction III. Genre, D. These prophecies demonstrate the unique
character of Hebrew scripture.

Special Topic: Inspiration

- Some translations take Micah 5:1 (i.e. Micah 4:14 in Hebrew text) with Micah 4 (cf. TEV). If so then it relates to
Micah 4:9-11a, where Jerusalem is attacked and exiled.

However, other translations take it with Micah 5:1-5a (NASB, NJB, NIV), which would form a contrast between

- Jerusalem with its faithless king and evil leaders

- Bethlehem with a great coming king and godly leader

- This chapter is very specific about the birthplace of the Messiah. Micah wrote in the eighth century B.C.
and precisely predicted the village of Jesus' birth. Some will deny the date of Micah, but if you do not accept the
750's then Micah was translated into Greek (i.e. the Septuagint in 250-150 B.C.; see Special Topic: Septuagint).
This is still well over a hundred fifty years before His birth.

The predictive element unique to the Bible shows:

- the inspiration of the Bible

- the sovereignty of YHWH over history

- the reality of the Messiahship of Jesus of Nazareth (Special Topic: The Bble (its uniqueness and inspiration)

The Jewish leaders were asked by Herod the Great where the Messiah was to be born (cf. Matt. 2) and they knew exactly the answer (Micah 5)!

- This chapter also hints at the pre-existence (see note at Micah 5:2, lines 4,5) of the Messiah as well as the
type of reign He will employ (Micah 5:4-5). This is shockingly specific prophecy. What a wonderful and accurate Bible we have been given by God.
